query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A high‐throughput, hybrid computational–experimental framework that integrates molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with calibrated interatomic potentials and CALPHAD-based thermodynamic modeling—both anchored by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements—can predict the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with a precision on the order of a few percent.
generation.material_initial_state: A disordered single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic or near-equiatomic FCC, BCC, or HCP solid solution) with a well-characterized chemical composition.
generation.intervention: Application of MD heating simulations to capture atomic rearrangements during melting along with concurrent DSC experiments for thermal analysis at controlled heating rates, combined with CALPHAD extrapolations from validated binary/ternary subsystems.
generation.conditions: Heating from room temperature to well above the solidus (in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation) under conditions replicable in MD (using accurate 2nd-nearest-neighbor or equivalent potentials) and DSC studies (with precise baseline and calibration), across a range of grain sizes and crystal structures typical for HEAs.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic structural rearrangements and short-range ordering (including grain boundary melting and chemical clustering) that mediate the transition from solid to liquid and influence volume change.
generation.mechanism: MD simulations capture the microscopic energy changes and rearrangements (e.g., pre-melting at grain boundaries, collective atomic diffusion) that lead to fusion; CALPHAD models extend these results by accounting for configurational and thermal entropy contributions based on lower-order systems; DSC measurements provide accurate, sample‐averaged enthalpy and entropy data for calibration. The combined output then yields liquid-phase thermodynamic properties by integrating structural snapshots with macroscopic thermal data.
generation.predicted_outcome: Melting temperatures will be predicted within ±5% error, latent heats and fusion entropies within a few kJ/mol and corresponding entropy units, and volume changes at melting within a couple of percent relative to experimental measurements. Liquid-phase thermodynamics (e.g., Gibbs free energy changes) will align with observed miscibility behavior from in‐situ imaging.
generation.baseline: Conventional single-technique approaches (e.g., using only DSC or traditional empirical estimates) typically yield larger uncertainties and less detailed insight into the melting process, particularly for complex, multi-component systems.
generation.boundary: This integrated method is expected to be applicable primarily to solid-solution based HEAs where reliable MD potentials and well-assessed CALPHAD databases exist. Its accuracy may be limited for alloys with significant intermetallic compound formation or amorphous phases where nonideal mixing effects become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis builds on separate findings: (1) MD simulation studies (e.g., PMC8956691) that detail atomistic melting mechanisms in refractory HEAs, and (2) DSC-based entropy and enthalpy determination studies (e.g., PMC7513177) plus CALPHAD assessments (e.g., PMC4366518). The new proposal is the specific integration and calibration of these approaches to cover the full range of melting properties across the HEA family; uncertainties remain regarding the transferability of MD interatomic potentials to all composition regimes and the extrapolation limits of CALPHAD for new multicomponent systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of HEAs covering different crystal structures (FCC, BCC, HCP) and compositions. Perform MD simulations using the recommended interatomic potentials combined with CALPHAD extrapolations to predict melting temperature, latent heat, fusion entropy, and volume change. Independently perform high-resolution DSC experiments and, where possible, in-situ imaging (e.g., neutron imaging) to measure these thermal properties. Compare predictions and measurements for each alloy.
measurements: Melting point (K) via DSC and in-situ imaging
Enthalpy of fusion (kJ/mol) from DSC integration
Entropy of fusion (J/(mol·K)) calculated from DSC curves
Volume change at melting (%) via density measurements or X-ray/neutron diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If for a significant majority (e.g., >70%) of tested HEAs the predicted melting temperature, fusion enthalpy or entropy, or volume change deviate from the experimental measurements by more than ~10% (i.e., outside the claimed few-percent error margin), then the integrated framework hypothesis is falsified.

Here we develop and apply this idea to quickly identify, screen and analyze structural alloys for use at moderate and high temperatures. We select a palette of 26 metallic elements that are most likely to produce the moderate and high-temperature properties ranges in MPEAs. The palette of elements is shown in Supplementary Table 1. Phase diagrams are the road maps for materials design, and give essential information on the phases present at a given alloy chemistry and temperature. Most binary and some ternary phase diagrams have been determined experimentally, but multi-component systems remain largely unexplored. Experimental measurement of multi-component phase diagrams is impractical due to the tremendous amount of work involved. In recent years, integration of the CALPHAD approach with key experiments has been demonstrated as an effective approach to determine complicated multi-component phase diagrams. The essence of the CALPHAD approach is to use experimental data from constituent binary and ternary phase diagrams to develop a thermodynamic database. AbstractWe determined the entropy of high entropy alloys by investigating single-crystalline nickel and five high entropy alloys: two fcc-alloys, two bcc-alloys and one hcp-alloy. Since the configurational entropy of these single-phase alloys differs from alloys using a base element, it is important to quantify the entropy. Using differential scanning calorimetry, cp-measurements are carried out from −170 °C to the materials’ solidus temperatures TS. From these experiments, we determined the thermal entropy and compared it to the configurational entropy for each of the studied alloys. We applied the rule of mixture to predict molar heat capacities of the alloys at room temperature, which were in good agreement with the Dulong-Petit law. The molar heat capacity of the studied alloys was about three times the universal gas constant, hence the thermal entropy was the major contribution to total entropy. The configurational entropy, due to the chemical composition and number of components, contributes less on the absolute scale. The melting mechanism of single crystal and polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) were investigated by the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using the second-nearest neighbor modified embedded-atom method (2NN MEAM) potential. For the single crystal RHEA, the density profile displays an abrupt drop from 11.25 to 11.00 g/cm3 at temperatures from 2910 to 2940 K, indicating all atoms begin significant local structural rearrangement. For polycrystalline RHEAs, a two-stage melting process is found. In the first melting stage, the melting of the grain boundary (GB) regions firstly occurs at the pre-melting temperature, which is relatively lower than the corresponding system-melting point. At the pre-melting temperature, most GB atoms have enough kinetic energies to leave their equilibrium positions, and then gradually induce the rearrangement of grain atoms close to GB. In the second melting stage at the melting point, most grain atoms have enough kinetic energies to rearrange, resulting in the chemical short-ranged order changes of all pairs.
